implementation_notes: Ruby's idiom is a one-liner: @summary ||= build_summary replaces the classic null-marker guard and is the standard memoisation form in Rails-era code. It is single-threaded-safe only in the weak sense that CRuby's GVL keeps the assignment itself atomic - the build can still be entered twice if it releases the GVL on I/O, and JRuby/TruffleRuby run it genuinely in parallel. Use `defined?(@summary) ? @summary : (@summary = build)` when the value may legitimately be false/nil, and a real primitive (Mutex, Concurrent::Map) when several threads can arrive first. The classic structure remains justified when the value must be reset (remove_instance_variable) or when no gem is available.
code_sketch:
class Report
  def summary
    @summary ||= Summary.build(rows)      # memoised on first call
  end
  # falsy-safe: defined?(@summary) ? @summary : (@summary = build)
  # reset:     remove_instance_variable(:@summary) if defined?(@summary)
end
pitfalls: ||= recomputes whenever the result is falsy: a builder returning nil/false (or an empty collection guarded by `||=`) looks like a cache miss on every call - the defined? form or a sentinel object is required.

Under a preemptive or GVL-releasing race two threads can both build; the second assignment wins and the first object is dropped (silently, since Ruby has no constructor-time uniqueness check) - use Mutex#synchronize or Concurrent::Map#compute_if_absent when that matters.
Memoised instance variables outlive the state they were derived from: after a config reload or a tenant switch the object serves stale data unless an explicit reset path exists.

Subclasses that override the builder inherit the cached value from a super call: reading `@cell` in a parent method can return a value built by different logic, so prefer an explicit cell accessor when overriding is expected.

variants.name: Thread-safe once-cell with Concurrent::Map / Mutex
variants.idiom_name: Concurrent::Map#compute_if_absent or Mutex#synchronize around the build
variants.implementation_notes: When the value is shared across threads, the idiomatic replacement for ||= is a real once-primitive from the concurrent-ruby gem - Concurrent::Map#compute_if_absent computes per key at most once and is the standard memo table - or, for a single value, an explicit Mutex plus a double-checked read. This variant keeps the same cell shape as the ||= form but moves the guarantee into a synchronisation object, which is what the language itself does not provide. Choose it whenever the object is reachable from more than one thread (Puma, Sidekiq, any threaded server).
pitfalls: compute_if_absent may run its block more than once under contention and publish one winner, so the block should be free of externally visible side effects (creating a connection twice is a leak).

Concurrent::Map is per-process: in multi-process deployments (Unicorn, clustered Puma) each worker memoises independently, so 'built once' never means 'built once globally' - and Fork-safety of an existing map or lock is a separate hazard.
A Mutex-guarded cell must be re-tested inside the lock (double-checked) or every waiter rebuilds the value, which is exactly the cost the memoisation was meant to remove.
